verses.1:
Al-Mizan explains that the Book is “wise” (ḥakīm) because it contains neither vanity nor falsehood. As guidance (hudā) and mercy (raḥmah) for the virtuous (muḥsinīn), it both directs people to true reality and conveys them to it; unlike vain speech (lahw al-kalām), it does not distract them from what should concern them and deprive them of blessings.

The virtuous maintain prayer and pay zakāt, the two most important deeds. Their certainty in the Hereafter entails certainty in divine unity and prophethood and generally god-fearing conduct. Thus the Book stands in sharp contrast to diversionary talk that keeps people from hearing it.

verses.6:
Al-Mizan explains diversion (lahw) as whatever distracts a person from what should concern him. Diversionary talk (lahw al-ḥadīth) includes speech that diverts from truth, such as mythical fables and vulgar tales, and speech that vies with it, such as poetry recitations, gatherings of vain amusement, and the playing of musical instruments.

The context suggests that Allah’s way (sabīl allāh) means the Qur’an, especially its accounts of the prophets and their peoples, which fanciful tales first oppose before weakening other teachings of truth in people’s eyes. The phrase “he takes it in derision” supports this: diversionary speech clashes with and ridicules truthful speech. The purchaser of such talk therefore appears to seek specifically to turn people from the Qur’an and mock it by portraying its speech and stories as no different from his own.

“Without any knowledge” (bi-ghayr ʿilmin) qualifies those who are led astray, though the misleaders too lack knowledge. The warning of humiliating punishment answers their derision: those who deride the Qur’an in worldly pride will themselves be derided and humiliated.
verses.7:
Al-Mizan takes the verse to describe the one who purchases diversionary talk in order to turn people from and ridicule the Qur’an. When God’s signs, meaning the Qur’an, are recited to him, he turns away arrogantly as though he hears nothing. A blockage (waqr) is a heavy load, as if he had filled his ears to prevent hearing; some regard it as an allusion to deafness. He is therefore threatened with a painful punishment.

Some explain the Arabic shifts between singular and plural pronouns by saying that the singular follows the word (lafẓ) while the plural follows its meaning (maʿnā). Al-Mizan considers it also possible that “them” in “for them there is a humiliating punishment” includes both the misleader and those he misleads; on this reading, the singular pronouns all refer to the purchaser of diversionary talk.
verses.8:
Al-Mizan explains that, after warning the purchaser of diversionary talk of humiliating and painful punishment, the Qur’an returns to the good news that believers who do righteous deeds will abide in gardens of bliss. God’s promise is true. Since the misleader tried to make the Qur’an seem like false legends and arrogantly disregarded its recitation, the verse stresses that God is All-mighty, who is never humiliated, and All-wise, whose speech contains no falsehood, idleness, or superstition.

The following description of the heavens, earth, animals, and plants establishes that God governs them because He created them, and is therefore able to promise paradise or punishment. “Without any pillars that you see” (tarawnahā) may clarify that the heavens have no pillars, as is evident, or specify that they have no visible pillars, implying invisible ones. The placement of firm mountains so that the earth does not shake implies a direct connection between mountains and earthquakes. God scattered every kind of walking animal upon the earth, and sent rain down to grow every noble, beneficial kind of plant; kind (zawj) also indicates that plants have genders. Some say the shift from “He” to “We” expresses God’s complete focus (ʿināyah) on this matter.

Having displayed God’s creation and governance, the Qur’an challenges the audience to show what the alleged gods have created. Their inability to do so proves God’s absolute oneness in divinity and lordship. Although they admit that God alone creates and claim only that their gods govern, Al-Mizan maintains that governance (tadbīr) is nothing other than creation (khalq): one who truly governs creates what he governs, and one who has created nothing governs nothing. Hence there is no god or lord except Allāh. The address, “Now show me what others besides Him have created,” apparently comes from the Prophet, since such an address is appropriate to him.

verses.12:
Al-Mizan explains ḥikmah as useful knowledge, opposed to ignorance (jahl) and pretence (jurbuzah). The command to give thanks to Allah is not a separate omitted statement, but explains what it means that Luqmān was given wisdom: true thanksgiving (shukr) is using a blessing properly in a way that points to its Source, which requires knowing both the Source and the blessing and how it should be used. Thus, granting Luqmān wisdom included inspiring and bidding him to give thanks.

The shift from “We” to “Allah” accords with divine unity: the first-person plural displays divine greatness, but thanksgiving cannot be directed to a plural expression. Thanksgiving benefits only the thankful person, while ingratitude harms only the ungrateful; Allah is absolutely self-sufficient (ghanī), receiving neither benefit nor harm from either response. He is all-laudable (ḥamīd), praised for His blessings regardless of how people receive them. The present tense for thanksgiving indicates that its benefit requires continuity, whereas the past tense for ingratitude indicates that even an occasional act of it is harmful.
verses.13: Al-Mizan explains that the greatness of an act follows from the magnitude of its effects and punishment. Since God is unequalled in greatness and magnificence and has no partner, disobeying Him by ascribing a partner to Him is the greatest misdeed. The unqualified description of polytheism as zulm ʿazīm means that it exceeds all other sins in gravity, immeasurably so.
verses.14:
Al-Mizan holds that this is a divine aside within the account of Luqmān’s sayings, not part of Luqmān’s speech. It establishes that gratitude to parents resembles, and is part of, gratitude to God, since God has enjoined it; thanking parents is therefore worship of God, and worship is thanksgiving to Him.

The mother’s successive weakness in carrying the child and the two years of suckling are mentioned to move one to thank parents, especially the mother. Wahnan may mean that she was in a state of weakness or that she became weak. Fiṣāl is the cessation of suckling, and its being “in two years” means that suckling lasts two years. Read alongside and his gestation and weaning take thirty months (46:15), this establishes a minimum pregnancy of six months.

The command to thank God and one’s parents explicates the injunction, while “To Me is the return” both warns and reinforces it. The shift from “We” to the third person has the same implication as in the preceding verse.
verses.15:
Al-Mizan explains that parents must not be obeyed when they press one to associate a partner with God. “That of which you have no knowledge” indicates that such a supposed partner is nonexistent, for what does not exist cannot be known; this reading may be supported by: Will you inform Allah about something He does not know in the heavens or on the earth? (10:18). Another view takes tushrik to mean takfur: parents must not be obeyed if they urge disbelief for which there is no proof, supported by the denial of authority to invented objects of worship in You do not worship besides Him but names that you and your fathers have invented, for which Allah has not sent down any authority (12:40).

Even so, one must accompany parents honourably and kindly in worldly affairs, bearing any hardship involved, but not follow them in religion unless they themselves turn penitently to God. The command to follow one who turns to God may thus refer to one’s parents if they have this quality, or to another person if they do not.

“In this world” limits honourable companionship to worldly matters rather than religion, makes its difficulties slight because worldly life is fleeting, and contrasts it with the eventual return to God. At that return, God will disclose the reality of people’s deeds and judge between them accordingly.
verses.16: Al-Mizan explains that “it” refers to good and evil, even if it is as slight as the weight of a mustard seed and hidden within a solid rock, the heavens, or the earth. God will bring it forth at Judgement, count it, and recompense it. After Luqmān’s teaching on divine unity, the verse turns to the Resurrection and Judgement: no deed, however minute or concealed, escapes God, for He is all-attentive, whose knowledge reaches the deepest hidden things, and all-aware, knowing the essence of all things.
verses.17:
Al-Mizan treats this and the following verses as Luqmān’s selection of righteous deeds and virtuous traits: prayer (ṣalāt), the pillar of faith; enjoining right and forbidding wrong; and patience (ṣabr) amid affliction. “That is indeed the steadiest of courses” refers specifically to patience, not to all the preceding commands. The distant demonstrative magnifies patience, and the Qur’an likewise calls patience the steadiest of courses in As for him who endures patiently and forgives that is indeed the steadiest of courses. (42:43) and …but if you are patient and Godwary, that is indeed the steadiest of courses (3:186).

According to al-Rāghib, ʿazm is setting the heart upon accomplishing something. Since ṣabr is self-restraint, it is a form of ʿazm: one whose heart remains fixed on a goal stays steadfast in pursuing it. Patience is therefore an essential faculty for preserving such resolve. The readings that take min ʿazm al-umūr to mean one of God’s resolute commands (ʿazīmah), or that equate ʿazm with jazm (“certainty”) in the dialect of Hudhayl, are rejected.
verses.18: Al-Mizan explains that turning one’s cheek askew means twisting the neck away in disdain, while maraḥ is excessive self-pleasure. The verse therefore forbids disdainfully turning one’s face from people and walking in self-exultant pride, for God does not love the conceited and boastful. The suggestion that it forbids bending one’s neck humbly when asking others for something does not fit the verse’s context.
verses.19: Al-Mizan explains qaṣd as moderation and ghaḍḍ as diminution. The verse commands moderation in one’s bearing while walking and a lowered volume while speaking, since the donkey’s voice is despised for its excessive loudness.
verses.20:
Al-Mizan takes the verse as returning to the argument before Luqmān’s story and primarily addressing idol-worshippers, though its ending can address people generally. Its first part may continue the Prophet’s preceding words, in which case there is no change of addressee. If God is instead the speaker, the shift from “they” to “you” expresses exasperation with people whose ignorance and obstinacy persist despite evidence; they are therefore directed to an immediately evident sign.

God’s disposing of the heavens and earth refers to the interconnected natural order governing the cosmos and human life. Since the human being, through awareness and will, is the noblest physical constituent, the cosmos is disposed for his sake. Taskhīr is the compelling of an instrument to act according to another’s will; the natural order follows God’s will and serves the order governing humanity. The lām in lakum apparently means “for your sake”: God employs the heavens and earth for humanity. It may instead mean ownership, so that human beings use them by God’s leave as civilization increasingly brings the world under their dominion, but this reading does not fit the opening, “Do you not see…?”

To shower (isbāgh) blessings means to supplement and expand them, and blessings (niʿam) are all benefits enjoyed by human beings. If the address is to polytheists, apparent blessings include the senses, limbs, health, and well-being, while hidden ones include imperceptible provisions such as awareness, will, and intellect. If it addresses everyone, apparent blessings may also include religion, which orders worldly and otherworldly affairs, and hidden blessings include spiritual stations attained through sincerity.

The final address apparently returns to the Prophet. Disputing (mujādalah) about God without knowledge, guidance, or an illuminating scripture means arguing over His oneness, lordship, and divinity without proof. Knowledge is acquired through rational proof; guidance is bestowed through revelation or inspiration; and scripture is the revealed divine book sent to prophets. These are the three paths to knowledge, with no fourth; those who lack them merely follow what others say.
verses.21:
Al-Mizan explains that “they” denotes those who dispute about God in the preceding verse. The summons to follow “what Allah has sent down,” rather than simply the Book or Qur’an, shows that it is not dogmatic: the Book’s divine origin is established by the proofs of prophethood. Thus, when they are called to divine unity through demonstrated evidence, they answer with baseless imitation of their fathers.

The question about Satan calling them to the punishment of the Blaze is a rebuke: will they follow their fathers even when this amounts to Satan’s summons to punishment? Even if… (law) is conjunctive, joined to an implied corresponding clause, so the challenge covers both whether Satan calls them or not. Following another is sound only when that person follows truth; following those upon falsehood, when it leads to misery and punishment, resembles worshipping other than God, whereas none is worthy of worship but Him.
verses.22:
Al-Mizan regards this as a new discussion, though it may also be a circumstantial qualifier of Satan’s calling: while Satan calls people toward punishment, the one who surrenders himself to God is saved and succeeds, because all affairs return to God and He alone should be worshipped.

To surrender one’s countenance (islām al-wajh) is to turn one’s whole being to God and away from all besides Him. Virtue (iḥsān) is righteous action based on certainty about the hereafter, as described in a guidance and mercy for the virtuous, who maintain the prayer, and pay the zakāt, and are certain of the Hereafter (31:3–4). The firmest handle is a hold that cannot break. Thus, whoever affirms God’s oneness and acts righteously with certainty of the hereafter will be saved and will not perish at the final outcome of his affair. The phrase “with Allah lies the outcome of all matters” explains why he has grasped such an unbreakable hold: the outcome belongs to the God who promises salvation and success.
verses.23:
Al-Mizan says these verses console the Prophet against grief over the faithless. They will return to God, who will inform them of their deeds by making their reality and consequences manifest to them in hellfire; He knows what is concealed in their breasts.

Their brief worldly provision before being driven to harsh punishment is another statement of this disclosure of their true condition. It also prevents the mistaken impression that their worldly comfort places them beyond God’s power until death or resurrection. They remain under His governance in every condition: He merely provides for them temporarily before taking them to punishment, and they can never thwart Him.

verses.25:
Al-Mizan holds that the verse shows both that divine unity belongs to human nature (fiṭrah) and that polytheists unwittingly confess it when they acknowledge God as creator of the heavens and earth. Creation entails governance: if God created the cosmos, He governs its affairs, grants and withholds blessings, and is the One hoped for and feared. He must therefore be the sole object of worship, without partner.

The Messenger is commanded to praise God for this unknowing confession: “All praise belongs to Allah!” Most do not understand what their admission entails. A small number do understand it fully but, like those described in They impugned them though they were convinced in their hearts wrongfully and defiantly. (27:14), obstinately refuse to submit to the truth.
verses.26:
Al-Mizan explains that confessing God as creator entails His exclusive lordship and divinity, since creation entails sole governance and disposal of the cosmos. The verse completes that argument and grounds it in a further proof: God is absolutely self-sufficient (ghanī) and utterly praiseworthy (maḥmūd).

As the source of all created things and every excellence, God possesses all that existents require; otherwise He could not be their source and benefactor. Since He is absolutely self-sufficient, everything in the heavens and earth belongs to Him, and He is its absolute sovereign. All cosmic events are under His direction. If another directed anything independently, that being would possess sovereignty over it, contradicting God’s absolute sovereignty. God is consequently Lord of the Worlds and the only One to be worshipped and thanked for blessings.

“To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth” establishes this oneness, while “the All-sufficient” explains His universal sovereignty. “The All-laudable” supplies a further argument: praise is due for beautiful acts done voluntarily, and every beauty in the world belongs ultimately to God. Therefore all praise returns to Him; if any part of the finely ordered world came from another independently of Him, praise would not belong wholly to Him.
verses.27:
Al-Mizan explains that “the trees of the earth” means every tree and “the sea” the entire sea; its replenishment by seven seas apparently signifies abundance rather than the precise number seven. God’s “words” (kalimāt) are meaningful utterances and can also denote what comes to be through His command, as in Whenever He wills something, he says to it Be! and it is (36:82).

Even if every tree became a pen and the sea, multiplied many times, became ink, the ink would be exhausted before God’s words were. His words and commands are never-ending. “Indeed Allah is all-mighty, all-wise” explains this: nothing can overcome Him, so what proceeds from Him cannot be exhausted; and in His wisdom He does not delegate the direction of the cosmos to another. The verse thus displays the extent of His dominion and the abundance of His cosmic commands, confirming that the direction of creation belongs to Him alone.
verses.28:
Al-Mizan turns here to the polytheists’ objection that resurrection is implausible because of the multitude of people who have died and decayed. Humanity’s creation and resurrection are to God as those of a single soul: multiplicity does not impede or distract Him, and there is no difference for Him between originating a thing and restoring it. Indeed, ease and difficulty do not properly apply to His acts.

The plural “your” stresses that all human beings, despite their number, are created and resurrected as readily as one soul. If people regard resurrection and recompense as difficult because of the innumerable and interwoven deeds to be judged, this assumes that God cannot distinguish them. But He is all-hearing of speech and all-seeing of deeds, directly aware of every outward act.

For this reason the verse concludes with these attributes rather than an explicit statement of power. It answers the question of how God can requite the many human words and deeds that no one could conceal from the all-hearing, all-seeing God. Knowledge of inward contents is answered instead by “Indeed Allah knows best what is in the breasts”; outward words and deeds are answered by His hearing and seeing. This distinction resembles: He said, Their knowledge is with my Lord, in a Book. My Lord neither makes any error nor forgets. (20:52).
verses.29:
Al-Mizan explains that the ordered interpenetration of night and day and the precisely timed courses of the sun and moon testify that their Governor cannot lack knowledge or awareness. God extends night into the hours of day and day into those of night, while each heavenly body repeatedly occupies its appointed positions for its specified term; such a consistent, finely adjusted system cannot arise from ignorance or chance.

Some commentators infer God’s awareness of human deeds simply from His knowledge of this cosmic order. Al-Mizan finds that explanation inadequate: the connection is only speculative, whereas “Have you not regarded…?” points to something that can be witnessed. The stronger reading considers the natural order underlying human action itself. A person observes how outward powers such as the senses and inward powers such as understanding and will; capacities and instruments; attraction and repulsion; and the successive stages of life are coordinated, each serving the others as the soul pursues its material perfection and happiness, though people may succeed or fail. Contemplating this intricate internal order makes it impossible to doubt that its Lord and Maker established it with knowledge and power. Witnessing the system that produces and orders human acts is therefore also witnessing that God is fully aware of what people do. And God knows best.
verses.30:
Al-Mizan says that the verse gathers the preceding claims—that all things originate from, depend on, and return to God, and that those invoked besides Him neither create nor command—under one principle: Allah alone is the Real (al-Ḥaqq), while what is invoked besides Him is nullity (al-Bāṭil). The Real is subsistent and abiding; nullity is evanescent and fleeting. The wording “Allah, He is the Real” conveys exclusivity: only He possesses subsistence without nullity.

God’s existence is absolute, unrestricted, unconditioned, necessary, and incapable of non-existence. Other beings are contingent, existing only through their cause; their existence is consequently limited and not necessary in itself. They subsist and are real only through God. Thus every thing, every natural order, and every lesser order in species and individuals depends on Him.

All perfections of existence—knowledge, power, life, hearing, seeing, unity, creation, sovereignty, self-sufficiency, praise, and awareness—subsist with God in a manner befitting His sanctity. Some, such as knowledge and power, are identical with His essence (dhāt); others, such as creation, sustenance, and mercy, are applied to His actions. Conversely, partnership in His essence or governance, and every implication of deficiency or need, are negated. These negative attributes (ṣifāt salbiyyah) include having no partner, number, physicality, time, place, ignorance, incapacity, nullity, or evanescence. His absolute existence negates all such deficiencies and thereby affirms it.

The All-exalted (al-ʿalī) may sum up the negative attributes, His transcendence beyond what does not befit Him, while the All-great (al-kabīr) sums up the positive attributes, His possession of every existent perfection. The opening and coda thus mutually establish that God is the locus of all perfection. The alleged deities have no reality or power to create or govern, because partnership with God in divinity or lordship is itself utter nullity. Accordingly, the Real corresponds to the Necessary Existent (wājib al-wujūd), the All-exalted to the negative attributes, and the All-great to the affirmative attributes (al-ṣifāt al-thubūtiyyah).
verses.31:
Al-Mizan explains the bāʾ in bi niʿmat Allāh as causal: ships travel upon the sea through God’s blessings, the means He provides, including wind, water, and other elements. Mentioning blessing prepares for the call to gratitude, since reason requires gratitude to one who confers benefit. Some commentators instead take the bāʾ as transitive or denoting accompaniment, referring to the goods carried on the ships.

The signs in this are for the abundantly patient (ṣabbār) and grateful (shakūr): the former bears hardship patiently, and the latter gives abundant thanks in ease. According to some commentators, this alludes to believers.
verses.32:
Al-Mizan, citing al-Rāghib, explains ẓullah, plural ẓulal, as an overshadowing raincloud, generally used in an ominous sense. The waves therefore surround seafarers like foreboding clouds, and in this extremity they cleave to God, pray for deliverance, and devote faith exclusively to Him. This manifests the human fiṭrah of belief in divine unity.

When God brings them safely to land, only some remain unswerving. Muqtaṣid denotes one proceeding straight toward his destination, here the divine unity to which fiṭrah guides; minhum indicates that these steadfast people are few. Most, by implication, do not persist in that faith. The one who impugns God’s signs is an ungrateful traitor: khattār is an intensive term for one repeatedly perfidious and disloyal, and the verse’s tone indicates that many are of this kind.
verses.33:
Al-Mizan treats this as the conclusion to the preceding proofs and admonitions, now addressed to all humanity. People are commanded to be wary of their Lord and fear Resurrection, when neither father nor child can suffice for the other; only faith and Godwariness will avail. Allah’s promise of that day is true.

“To repay” (jazāʾ) means to suffice or avail. Worldly life must not beguile people with its attractions, nor may the Deceiver beguile them concerning God. The Deceiver can mean the whole class of things that deceive human beings in worldly life, or Satan specifically; commentators give both possibilities. Thus the warning is against being deluded by worldly trinkets or by any deceiving influence into neglecting God and the certain Resurrection.
verses.34:
Al-Mizan explains that God lists three matters within His knowledge: the Hour, whose knowledge He reserves exclusively to Himself; the sending down of rain; and what is in wombs, which others may also know. He then states two matters unknown to every soul—what it will earn tomorrow and in what land it will die—through which human beings’ ignorance of all that will befall them is made clear.

The point is that God knows every great and small affair, including the Hour, which no creature can know, whereas people do not know even crucial matters concerning themselves. They are therefore warned not to associate partners with Him, rebel against His command, or turn away from His summons, lest ignorance bring about their ruin.
